Discovering Customer Segments and Product Associations — a KDD Project¶

Author: Meron Tesfandrias · Course: CMPE 255 · Repo: MeronDT/CMPE-255-Data-Mining-process · App: cmpe-255-data-mining-process-retail-segments.streamlit.app

Data: Online Retail II — UCI Machine Learning Repository (dataset 502, CC BY 4.0), donated by D. Chen. Transaction lines of a UK-based online retailer of giftware (many customers are wholesalers), 1 Dec 2009 – 9 Dec 2011: 1,067,371 lines in the two Excel sheets, of which 22,523 are repeated across the sheets, so 1,044,848 distinct lines. Mirrored on Kaggle as mashlyn/online-retail-ii-uci; the notebook downloads the original from UCI (no login needed).

KDD (Fayyad, Piatetsky-Shapiro & Smyth, 1996) is "the nontrivial process of identifying valid, novel, potentially useful, and ultimately understandable patterns in data". It defines nine steps, usually grouped into five stages:

Stage Fayyad's steps In this notebook
0 · Domain & goals 1. Understand the application domain, prior knowledge and the end user's goals business context, two discovery goals, evaluation plan and pass marks
1 · Selection 2. Create a target data set load both sheets once each, define equal 12-month discovery and validation periods
2 · Preprocessing 3. Data cleaning and preprocessing cancellations (matched one-to-one within each period), non-product codes, invalid prices, duplicates, missing customers
3 · Transformation 4. Data reduction and projection customer RFM table (log, scaling, PCA); invoice × product basket matrix
4 · Data mining 5. Match goals to a mining method · 6. Choose algorithms · 7. Mine K-means segmentation · FP-Growth association rules
5 · Interpretation / Evaluation 8. Interpret mined patterns profile segments and rules; test them on the next year's data against baselines
→ Act 9. Act on the discovered knowledge consolidated outputs + a web app for marketing staff

Headline results:

  • Segments. Four customer segments that are stable (out-of-bag bootstrap ARI 0.92) and separate next year's behaviour sharply. The top 17 % of customers ("Champions") produced 64 % of revenue, and 96 % of them bought again the following year, against 40 % of "Lapsed one-off buyers". But they are a useful partition, not natural clusters, and a plain RFM score ranks next-year activity better (AUC 0.765 vs 0.739, gap CI +0.018 to +0.034). So the segments are delivered as explainable labels, with the RFM score beside them as the ranking tool.
  • Rules. 325 associations (598 directional rules). 59 % of the rules meet all three thresholds (support, confidence, lift) again in the following year, against 12 % for rules just below the thresholds. The stable ones are mostly variants of the same product. The few genuinely cross-product associations, matching-design sets such as red spotty paper napkins + cups → plates (84 % confidence, 90 % the next year), are the novel part, but only about a quarter of them hold up the next year.
  • Delivery. Both are delivered in a web app for marketing staff, which ships exactly the segmentation that was validated.

How to run: Runtime → Run all (≈ 4–7 min on free Colab; most of it is downloading and reading the 44 MB Excel file once — later runs use a cache). Every figure, table and the app are written to artifacts/.

            "rules_hold_all_thresholds": 0.50}     # >= 50 % of rules meet support, confidence AND lift again next year

Stage 0 — Understanding the application domain and the KDD goals¶

Fayyad step 1: learn the domain and the relevant prior knowledge, and identify the end user's goals.

Domain and prior knowledge¶

The data come from a UK-based, store-less online retailer selling mainly unique all-occasion giftware (tableware, Christmas decorations, bags, children's items). Many customers are wholesalers who resell the products, so order sizes vary enormously, and sales are strongly seasonal, peaking in September–November ahead of Christmas. Chen, Sain & Guo (2012) first analysed the 2010-11 part of this data with RFM-based segmentation, which is the established retail practice:

  • RFM (recency, frequency, monetary value) is the standard, explainable way to group customers by purchasing behaviour; recent, frequent, high-spending customers are the most valuable and most likely to buy again. A simple RFM score is therefore the baseline the segments must be compared with.
  • Market-basket analysis (Agrawal et al., 1993) finds products bought together; it underpins "customers also bought" recommendations and store/catalogue layout. The retailer designs its products in collections (e.g. "red retrospot"), so matching items bought together are partly expected.

End-user goals → discovery goals¶

End user Business goal KDD goal (descriptive, not predictive)
Marketing manager target campaigns at the right customers G1 — discover customer segments from purchasing behaviour that each call for a different action
Merchandising / web team increase basket size with cross-selling G2 — discover product associations ("customers who buy X also buy Y")

How the patterns will be evaluated (Fayyad's four criteria)¶

Criterion Test used here Pass mark (set in revision 2)
Valid patterns found in the discovery year must still hold in the following year. Segments must separate next-year activity and spend; rules must meet support, confidence and lift again segments rank next-year activity at least as well as an RFM score; ≥ 50 % of rules meet all three thresholds next year, clearly more than near-miss rules
Novel rules are split into obvious variants (same product, other colour/design) and genuinely cross-product associations, and the split is audited by hand; findings are compared with what the merchandiser already knows (the collections) — (argued, not scored)
Potentially useful each segment gets a concrete action and the revenue at stake; validated rules feed a recommendation tool; how many products and baskets the rules reach —
Understandable segments described in plain words against customer tertiles; rules shown as readable product names —

The pass marks were added in revision 2, before the re-run with the corrected cleaning but after the first run's results were known. They are documented targets, not blind ones.

Stage 1 — Selection¶

Fayyad step 2: select the data set, or subset of variables and records, on which discovery will be performed.

    print({name: len(s) for name, s in sheets.items()})

    raw = raw[~overlap].drop(columns="sheet").reset_index(drop=True)

    raw["InvoiceDate"] = pd.to_datetime(raw["InvoiceDate"])
    raw.to_pickle(cache)

Target data set¶

Decision Choice Rationale
Records every transaction line once: the 2009-10 sheet runs to 9 Dec 2010 and the 2010-11 sheet starts on 1 Dec 2010, so the 22,523 repeated lines (1–9 Dec 2010) are dropped at load time, before any cleaning full history, no double counting
Attributes invoice, product code, quantity, date, price and customer for RFM and baskets; description as the product label; country descriptive only every attribute has a role
Discovery period 1 Dec 2009 – 30 Nov 2010 (12 months) one full seasonal cycle to mine patterns
Validation period 1 Dec 2010 – 30 Nov 2011 (12 months) an equally long, untouched year to test whether patterns are valid. The last 9 days (1–9 Dec 2011, the partial month on the chart) are used only for the deployed app
Segmentation scope lines with a Customer ID RFM needs a customer
Basket scope all invoices (with or without Customer ID) an anonymous basket is still a basket. Anonymous invoices are larger (2.4), so 5.3 checks that they do not drive the rules

No information crosses the split. Every data-dependent cleaning rule (matching cancellations to purchases) runs within each period, so nothing from the validation year changes the discovery year.

Stage 2 — Preprocessing¶

Fayyad step 3: basic operations such as removing noise, deciding how to handle missing data, and accounting for known changes.

df = raw.copy(); log = []
def step(action, mask_removed):
    global df
    log.append({"action": action, "lines_removed": int(mask_removed.sum()), "lines_left": int((~mask_removed).sum())})
    df = df[~mask_removed]
period_of = lambda d: np.select([d["InvoiceDate"] < DISCOVERY_END, d["InvoiceDate"] < VALIDATION_END], ["discovery", "validation"], "after")

is_cancel = df["Invoice"].str.startswith("C")
cancellations = df[is_cancel].copy()
step("Separate cancellation lines (invoice starts with 'C')", is_cancel)

# Remove purchases that were cancelled in full: each cancellation is matched to ONE purchase - the most recent EARLIER
# purchase by the same customer of the same product and quantity, within the SAME period (no information crosses
# the discovery/validation boundary). Unmatched cancellations (partial returns) feed the return_rate feature.
pur = df[df["Customer ID"].notna()][["Customer ID", "StockCode", "Quantity", "InvoiceDate"]].assign(pid=lambda d: d.index)
can = cancellations[cancellations["Customer ID"].notna()][["Customer ID", "StockCode", "Quantity", "InvoiceDate"]] \
          .assign(Quantity=lambda d: -d["Quantity"], cid=lambda d: d.index)
pur["period"], can["period"] = period_of(pur), period_of(can)
match = pd.merge_asof(can.sort_values("InvoiceDate"), pur.sort_values("InvoiceDate"), on="InvoiceDate",
                      by=["Customer ID", "StockCode", "Quantity", "period"], direction="backward").dropna(subset=["pid"])
match = match.drop_duplicates("pid")                                    # one purchase can absorb only one cancellation
cancellations["matched"] = cancellations.index.isin(match["cid"])
print(f"{len(can):,} cancellation lines with a customer: {cancellations['matched'].sum():,} matched one-to-one to an earlier purchase, "
      f"{(~cancellations['matched'] & cancellations['Customer ID'].notna()).sum():,} unmatched (partial returns, adjustments, older purchases)")
step("Remove purchases cancelled in full (one-to-one, earlier purchase, same period)", df.index.isin(match["pid"]))

non_product = ~df["StockCode"].str.match(r"^\d{5}")         # POST, DOT, M, BANK CHARGES, AMAZONFEE, TEST...
print("Non-product codes removed:", sorted(df.loc[non_product, "StockCode"].unique())[:25], "...")
step("Remove non-product codes (postage, fees, manual adjustments, tests)", non_product)
step("Remove lines with quantity <= 0 or price <= 0", (df["Quantity"] <= 0) | (df["Price"] <= 0))
dupes = df.duplicated()
print(f"Exact duplicates: {dupes.sum():,} lines = {(df.loc[dupes, 'Quantity'] * df.loc[dupes, 'Price']).sum() / (df['Quantity'] * df['Price']).sum():.1%} of revenue; "
      f"{df.loc[dupes, 'Invoice'].nunique():,} invoices affected")
step("Remove exact duplicate lines (same invoice, product, quantity, price and second)", dupes)

# One description per product (codes have spelling variants / damaged-stock notes); missing descriptions stay missing
df["Description"] = df["Description"].replace("nan", np.nan)
canonical = df.groupby("StockCode")["Description"].agg(lambda s: s.value_counts().index[0] if s.notna().any() else "UNKNOWN")
df["Description"] = df["StockCode"].map(canonical)
df["Revenue"] = df["Quantity"] * df["Price"]
df["period"] = period_of(df)

# Returns for the return_rate feature: product-code cancellations that did NOT cancel a purchase in full
returns = cancellations[~cancellations["matched"] & cancellations["StockCode"].str.match(r"^\d{5}") & (cancellations["Price"] > 0)].copy()
returns["value"] = -returns["Quantity"] * returns["Price"]; returns["period"] = period_of(returns)

preprocessing_log = pd.DataFrame(log); preprocessing_log.to_csv(REP / "preprocessing_log.csv", index=False)
display(preprocessing_log)
print(f"Clean: {len(df):,} lines, {df['Invoice'].nunique():,} invoices, {df['StockCode'].nunique():,} products, "
      f"{df['Customer ID'].nunique():,} customers; {df['Customer ID'].isna().mean():.1%} of lines have no customer")

Preprocessing decisions¶

  • Cancellations (19,165 lines) are separated, not netted. A cancellation is a different event from a purchase, and netting would hide it. Each cancellation is matched to one purchase: the most recent earlier purchase by the same customer of the same product and quantity, within the same period. That removes 5,825 purchases cancelled in full. (The first version matched across periods, ignored time order and removed every matching purchase: 13,653 lines.) The 12,621 unmatched cancellations (partial returns, or cancellations of older purchases) feed return_rate. It uses product codes only, excludes the fully cancelled purchases, and is measured as returned value ÷ gross product spend.
  • Non-product codes (4,661 lines) — postage (POST, DOT), bank charges, Amazon fees, manual adjustments (M, ADJUST), samples, tests and DCGS… gift codes — are not products and would create meaningless rules ("postage → postage").
  • Zero/negative quantity or price (5,937 lines) are stock corrections, damaged/lost goods and free items, not sales.
  • Exact duplicates (11,622 lines, 0.3 % of revenue, on 4,285 invoices) — identical invoice, product, quantity, price and second — are treated as double entries. Baskets are binary, so rules are unaffected. (Before the sheet overlap was removed at load time, this step also caught the 22k repeated lines, which made duplicates look three times more common than they are.)
  • Missing Customer ID (22.7 % of clean lines): kept for basket analysis, excluded from segmentation (RFM needs a customer). Anonymous invoices are larger (mean 77 products vs 21; 99th percentile 566 vs 102) and cheaper per invoice (median £184 vs £301), probably trade or batch orders. 5.3 re-mines the rules without them.
  • Extreme lines: the largest lines (e.g. 9,360 rotating silver-angel T-light holders for £15,818) look like genuine wholesale orders, and the highest unit prices are real furniture (a vintage kitchen cabinet at £295). They are kept, because the log transformation in Stage 3 limits their influence on clustering.

Result: 997,638 clean lines, 39,266 invoices, 4,699 products, 5,842 identified customers.

🔍 Critic review — Preprocessing¶

Each stage was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process as defined by Fayyad, Piatetsky-Shapiro and Smyth, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on KDD and data mining. Review the Preprocessing stage of my retail KDD project below. Check it against everything this KDD stage requires. Focus especially on: whether every cleaning rule is justified by an observed data problem, how missing customer IDs and cancellations are handled, and whether any rule could silently bias the segments or rules. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Cancellations matched only on exact customer/product/quantity; are the 33k duplicate lines really errors? Partial returns captured by return_rate; duplicates identical to the second, baskets binary so rules unaffected — documented.
2 Cancellation matching many-to-one, ignored time; return_rate double-counted; duplicates unexamined. One-to-one, time-ordered, within-period matching (5,825 lines); return_rate rebuilt; duplicate revenue share reported.
3 Most "duplicates" were the sheet overlap. With the overlap removed, true duplicates are 11,622 lines (0.3 % of revenue).

Stage 3 — Transformation¶

Fayyad step 4: find useful features to represent the data, using dimensionality reduction or transformation methods.

3.1 Customer table (for G1): RFM and behavioural features¶

In [7]:
def customer_features(lines, returns, snapshot):
    """One row per customer, measured at `snapshot` (the day after the period ends)."""
    c = lines.dropna(subset=["Customer ID"]).groupby("Customer ID")
    f = pd.DataFrame({
        "recency_days": (snapshot - c["InvoiceDate"].max()).dt.days,
        "frequency": c["Invoice"].nunique(),
        "monetary": c["Revenue"].sum(),
        "tenure_days": (snapshot - c["InvoiceDate"].min()).dt.days,
        "distinct_products": c["StockCode"].nunique(),
        "country": c["Country"].agg(lambda s: s.mode()[0]),
    })
    f["avg_basket_value"] = f["monetary"] / f["frequency"]
    returned = returns.groupby("Customer ID")["value"].sum().reindex(f.index).fillna(0)
    f["return_rate"] = returned / (f["monetary"] + returned)      # share of gross product spend that was returned
    return f

disc_lines = df[df["period"] == "discovery"]
val_lines = df[df["period"] == "validation"]
customers = customer_features(disc_lines, returns[returns["period"] == "discovery"], DISCOVERY_END)
print(f"{len(customers):,} customers in the discovery period"); display(customers.describe().T.round(2))

from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

SEGMENT_FEATURES = ["recency_days", "frequency", "monetary"]          # classic RFM - see the critic prompt about alternatives
projector = Pipeline([("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p)), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
Z = projector.fit_transform(customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES].plot.box(ax=axes[0], logy=True, title="Raw RFM: heavily skewed (log axis)")
pd.DataFrame(Z, columns=SEGMENT_FEATURES).plot.box(ax=axes[1], title="After log1p + standardisation")
savefig("transformation_rfm")
print("Correlation of transformed RFM features:"); display(pd.DataFrame(Z, columns=SEGMENT_FEATURES).corr().round(2))
pca = PCA(2).fit(Z); print(f"2-D PCA projection keeps {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.0%} of the variance (used for plots)")

Correlation of transformed RFM features:
recency_days frequency monetary
recency_days 1.00 -0.48 -0.42
frequency -0.48 1.00 0.81
monetary -0.42 0.81 1.00 
2-D PCA projection keeps 94% of the variance (used for plots)

Why these transformations. Frequency and monetary value span several orders of magnitude (1 to 174 orders; £2 to £319k per customer) and are right-skewed, while K-means uses Euclidean distance, so a handful of wholesalers would dominate untransformed data. log1p compresses the scale and standardisation gives each RFM dimension equal weight. Only three features are used so each segment can be explained in one sentence.

Caveat, tested in 5.2: frequency and monetary still correlate at 0.81 after transformation, so purchase volume is effectively weighted twice. 5.2 clusters an alternative representation (recency + one averaged volume factor). It agrees with the main segmentation at ARI 0.73 and predicts next year no better, so RFM is kept. Recency's log scale stretches the first weeks, but the tertile labels and next-year results show that cooling and lapsed customers are still separated. Wholesalers are not modelled separately: customers with an average basket above £1,000 are only 0.7–8.4 % of each segment (5.1). The 2-D PCA projection keeps 94 % of the variance, so the plots in Stage 5 are faithful.

3.2 Basket matrix (for G2): invoice × product¶

In [9]:
item_name = df.drop_duplicates("StockCode").set_index("StockCode")["Description"]
dup = item_name.duplicated(keep=False)
item_name[dup] = item_name[dup] + " (" + item_name[dup].index + ")"        # keep labels unique

def item_support(lines):
    """Share of invoices that contain each product."""
    l = lines.assign(item=lines["StockCode"].map(item_name))
    return (l.groupby("item")["Invoice"].nunique() / l["Invoice"].nunique()).sort_values(ascending=False)

def basket_matrix(lines, items):
    """Boolean invoice x product matrix restricted to `items`; keeps EVERY invoice so support is relative to all baskets."""
    l = lines.assign(item=lines["StockCode"].map(item_name))
    b = l[l["item"].isin(items)].groupby(["Invoice", "item"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0) > 0
    return b.reindex(index=l["Invoice"].unique(), columns=items, fill_value=False)

disc_support = item_support(disc_lines)
frequent_items = disc_support[disc_support >= MIN_SUPPORT].index
disc_baskets = basket_matrix(disc_lines, frequent_items)
basket_sizes = disc_lines.groupby("Invoice")["StockCode"].nunique()
print(f"{disc_lines['Invoice'].nunique():,} invoices x {disc_lines['StockCode'].nunique():,} products -> reduced to {len(frequent_items)} products "
      f"with support >= {MIN_SUPPORT:.0%}; matrix {disc_baskets.shape[0]:,} x {disc_baskets.shape[1]} ({disc_baskets.values.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB)")
print("Distinct products per invoice:", basket_sizes.describe(percentiles=[.5, .9, .99]).round(0)[["50%", "90%", "99%", "max"]].to_dict())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
disc_support.head(15).sort_values().plot.barh(ax=axes[0], color="#55A868", title="Most frequently purchased products (share of invoices)")
axes[1].loglog(np.arange(1, len(disc_support) + 1), disc_support.to_numpy(), c="#4C72B0")
axes[1].axhline(MIN_SUPPORT, c="r", ls="--", label=f"min support {MIN_SUPPORT:.0%} -> {len(frequent_items)} products kept")
axes[1].set(title="Long tail: support of every product, by rank", xlabel="product rank", ylabel="share of invoices"); axes[1].legend()
savefig("transformation_item_support")

19,616 invoices x 4,047 products -> reduced to 714 products with support >= 1%; matrix 19,616 x 714 (14 MB)
Distinct products per invoice: {'50%': 15.0, '90%': 49.0, '99%': 177.0, 'max': 577.0}

Why this reduction is safe. An itemset can only be frequent if every item in it is frequent (the Apriori property). Removing the 3,333 products that appear in fewer than 1 % of invoices therefore loses no possible rule at this support level. It shrinks the matrix from 4,047 to 714 products (14 MB), which makes FP-Growth run in seconds. Every invoice is kept, so support is measured against all 19,616 discovery-year baskets. The long-tail chart shows the cost: most of the catalogue can never appear in a rule at 1 % support. 5.3 measures that coverage and tries other thresholds. A typical invoice has 15 distinct products (90th percentile 49, 99th 177).

Stage 4 — Data mining¶

Fayyad steps 5–7: match the goals to a mining method, choose the algorithms and parameters, and search for patterns.

Goal Method (step 5) Algorithm (step 6) Why
G1 segments clustering K-means on log-RFM fast, simple to explain, centroids are readable profiles. k is chosen with silhouette, plus out-of-bag bootstrap stability for every k
G2 associations association-rule mining FP-Growth + rule generation same output as Apriori but without candidate generation — much faster on wide baskets. Thresholds: 1 % support, 40 % confidence, lift 3. 5.3 tests the alternatives

Choosing k. Silhouette is highest at k = 2 (0.41), but two groups only split active from inactive customers, which is too coarse to act on. Within 3–6, k = 4 has the best silhouette (0.34) and the best out-of-bag stability (ARI 0.92, worst resample 0.85); from k = 5 the worst resample drops to 0.55. A silhouette of 0.34 and the PCA plot (one continuous cloud) show these are a useful partition of a continuum, not natural clusters. G1 is worded accordingly.

4.1 Customer segmentation (step 7, G1)¶

In [10]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score

k_search = []
for k in range(2, 11):
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Z)
    k_search.append({"k": k, "inertia": km.inertia_, "silhouette": silhouette_score(Z, km.labels_, sample_size=4000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)})
k_search = pd.DataFrame(k_search)

# Stability of each k: refit on bootstrap resamples and compare labels on the OUT-OF-BAG customers only
def oob_stability(k, n_boot=20):
    base = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Z).labels_
    rng, aris = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE), []
    for b in range(n_boot):
        inb = rng.integers(0, len(Z), len(Z)); oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(Z)), inb)
        aris.append(adjusted_rand_score(base[oob], KMeans(k, n_init=5, random_state=b).fit(Z[inb]).predict(Z[oob])))
    return np.mean(aris), np.min(aris)
k_search[["oob_ari_mean", "oob_ari_min"]] = [oob_stability(k) for k in k_search["k"]]
k_search = k_search.round(4); k_search.to_csv(REP / "k_selection.csv", index=False); display(k_search)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.plot(k_search["k"], k_search["inertia"], marker="o"); ax.set(xlabel="k", ylabel="inertia")
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.plot(k_search["k"], k_search["silhouette"], marker="s", c="#C44E52", label="silhouette")
ax2.plot(k_search["k"], k_search["oob_ari_mean"], marker="^", c="#55A868", label="bootstrap stability (ARI)"); ax2.legend(loc="center right")

4.2 Association rules (step 7, G2)¶

In [12]:
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import fpgrowth, association_rules

def mine_rules(baskets, min_support=MIN_SUPPORT, min_conf=MIN_CONFIDENCE, min_lift=MIN_LIFT):
    itemsets = fpgrowth(baskets, min_support=min_support, use_colnames=True, max_len=3)
    r = association_rules(itemsets, num_itemsets=len(baskets), metric="confidence", min_threshold=min_conf)
    r = r[r["lift"] >= min_lift].copy()
    r["antecedents"] = r["antecedents"].apply(lambda s: tuple(sorted(s)))
    r["consequents"] = r["consequents"].apply(lambda s: tuple(sorted(s)))
    r["itemset"] = [tuple(sorted(a + c)) for a, c in zip(r["antecedents"], r["consequents"])]
    return itemsets, r.sort_values(["lift", "confidence"], ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

t0 = time.time()
itemsets, rules = mine_rules(disc_baskets)
print(f"{len(itemsets):,} frequent itemsets -> {len(rules):,} rules with confidence >= {MIN_CONFIDENCE} and lift >= {MIN_LIFT} "
      f"({time.time() - t0:.0f}s). They come from {rules['itemset'].nunique()} distinct itemsets: most pairs appear as A->B and B->A.")
display(rules.drop_duplicates("itemset")[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift"]].head(10).round(3))

Stage 5 — Interpretation / Evaluation¶

Fayyad step 8: interpret the mined patterns, possibly returning to earlier steps, and judge them against the criteria set in Stage 0.

5.1 Segment profiles (understandable)¶

In [13]:
# Describe segments against customer TERTILES. Each label is the tertile that holds MOST of the segment's members,
# with that share shown, so a segment whose median sits just above a cut-off is not called "high" without qualification.
q = customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES + ["tenure_days"]].quantile([1 / 3, 2 / 3])
def tertile(col, v):
    return np.where(v <= q.loc[1 / 3, col], 0, np.where(v > q.loc[2 / 3, col], 2, 1))
NAMES = {"recency_days": ["active", "cooling", "lapsed"], "frequency": ["one-off", "repeat", "frequent"],
         "monetary": ["low-spend", "mid-spend", "high-spend"]}
def describe_members(g):
    parts = []
    for col, names in NAMES.items():
        shares = np.bincount(tertile(col, g[col]), minlength=3) / len(g)
        parts.append(f"{names[shares.argmax()]} {shares.max():.0%}")
    return " · ".join(parts + ([f"new {(g['tenure_days'] <= 90).mean():.0%}"] if (g["tenure_days"] <= 90).mean() >= .5 else []))

def profile_segments(c):
    p = c.groupby("cluster").agg(customers=("frequency", "size"), recency_days=("recency_days", "median"),
                                 frequency=("frequency", "median"), monetary=("monetary", "median"),
                                 avg_basket_value=("avg_basket_value", "median"), tenure_days=("tenure_days", "median"),
                                 return_rate=("return_rate", "mean"), non_UK_share=("country", lambda s: (s != "United Kingdom").mean()),
                                 basket_over_1000_share=("avg_basket_value", lambda s: (s > 1000).mean()), revenue=("monetary", "sum"))
    p["revenue_share_%"] = (p["revenue"] / p["revenue"].sum() * 100).round(1)
    p["customer_share_%"] = (p["customers"] / p["customers"].sum() * 100).round(1)
    p["profile"] = [describe_members(c[c["cluster"] == k]) for k in p.index]
    return p

prof = profile_segments(customers).sort_values("monetary", ascending=False)
prof["segment"] = [f"S{i + 1}" for i in range(len(prof))]
SEGMENT_OF = prof["segment"].to_dict(); customers["segment"] = customers["cluster"].map(SEGMENT_OF)
prof = prof.set_index("segment").round(3); prof.to_csv(REP / "segment_profiles.csv")
print("Tertile cut-offs used for the labels:"); display(q.round(1))
display(prof.drop(columns="revenue"))

# Baselines: do the clusters predict next year better than the standard tools they are meant to improve on?
# Each segmentation is scored by how well its ORDER of groups ranks next-year activity (AUC) and next-year revenue.
rank_score = lambda x: pd.Series(x, index=customers.index).rank(pct=True)
r_s, f_s, m_s = rank_score(-customers["recency_days"]), rank_score(customers["frequency"]), rank_score(customers["monetary"])
rfm_score = r_s + f_s + m_s
alt = KMeans(K, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(np.c_[Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1:].mean(axis=1)])   # R + one 'volume' factor
alt_rank = pd.Series(alt.labels_, index=customers.index).map(
    customers.assign(l=alt.labels_).groupby("l")["monetary"].median().rank(ascending=False))
candidates = {
    f"K-means on log-RFM (k={K}, the project's segments)": -customers["segment"].str[1].astype(int),
    "Alternative: K-means on recency + one volume factor": -alt_rank,
    "RFM score (sum of R, F, M percentile ranks), quartiles": pd.qcut(rfm_score, 4, labels=False),
    "Monetary tertiles": pd.qcut(customers["monetary"], 3, labels=False),
    "RFM score, continuous (upper bound for a score)": rfm_score,
}
active = (fut > 0).astype(int)
baseline_table = pd.DataFrame([{"segmentation": n, "groups": int(s.nunique()) if s.nunique() < 20 else None,
                                "AUC_active_next_year": roc_auc_score(active, s), "spearman_next_year_revenue": spearmanr(s, fut)[0]}
                               for n, s in candidates.items()]).set_index("segmentation").round(3)
baseline_table.to_csv(REP / "segment_baselines.csv"); display(baseline_table)
print("Agreement between the two K-means variants (ARI):", round(adjusted_rand_score(customers["cluster"], alt.labels_), 3))
km_s, rfm_q = candidates[list(candidates)[0]].to_numpy(), candidates[list(candidates)[2]].to_numpy(); act = active.to_numpy()
bidx = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE).integers(0, len(act), (500, len(act)))
gap = [roc_auc_score(act[i], rfm_q[i]) - roc_auc_score(act[i], km_s[i]) for i in bidx]
print(f"AUC gap, RFM-score quartiles minus K-means segments: {np.mean(gap):+.3f} (95 % bootstrap CI {np.quantile(gap, .025):+.3f} to {np.quantile(gap, .975):+.3f})")

Do the segments predict next year? They were built only from 2009-10 behaviour, yet they sharply separate who buys in 2010-11:

Segment Active next year Median spend next year
Champions 96 % £2,493
S2 74 % £560
New customers 65 % £256
Lapsed one-off buyers 40 % £0

The ordering of the segments is exactly the ordering of their future value. Among discovery-year customers, Champions produced 66 % of next year's revenue and S2 21 %. Those returning customers produced 70 % of all next-year revenue (the rest came from new customers and anonymous invoices), so the Champions alone account for 47 % of everything the shop sold the next year. Reactivating "cooling" S2 customers (£1.37 M next-year revenue at stake) is worth more than chasing lapsed ones (£0.36 M).

But do they beat the standard tool? No. The pre-set pass mark is not met. Scored by how well the order of the groups ranks next-year activity:

Segmentation AUC Spearman ρ with next-year revenue
RFM-score quartiles (sum of R, F and M percentile ranks) 0.765 0.601
K-means segments (this project) 0.739 0.575
Monetary tertiles 0.729 0.586
Continuous RFM score (an upper bound) 0.783 0.628

The clusters predict better than spend alone, but not better than a plain RFM score. An alternative clustering on recency + one volume factor (the Stage 3 caveat) does no better (0.745) and agrees with the main one at ARI 0.73. Conclusion: the segments are valid as descriptions. They are stable, they order next-year value correctly, and each maps to a distinct action. For ranking customers within a campaign, the RFM score is the better tool. The app therefore pairs each customer's segment with the recency, frequency and spend values behind it.

5.3 Are the rules valid? Re-measure each rule on the following year¶

In [17]:
val_baskets = basket_matrix(val_lines, items=frequent_items)
def rule_stats(baskets, a, c):
    has_a = baskets[list(a)].all(axis=1); has_c = baskets[list(c)].all(axis=1)
    sup_a, sup_c, sup_ac = has_a.mean(), has_c.mean(), (has_a & has_c).mean()
    conf = sup_ac / sup_a if sup_a else np.nan
    return pd.Series({"val_support": sup_ac, "val_confidence": conf, "val_lift": conf / sup_c if sup_c else np.nan})
add_validation = lambda r: r.join(r.apply(lambda x: rule_stats(val_baskets, x["antecedents"], x["consequents"]), axis=1))

rules = add_validation(rules)
# A rule HOLDS next year only if it meets ALL THREE discovery thresholds again: support, confidence and lift
rules["holds_strict"] = (rules["val_support"] >= MIN_SUPPORT) & (rules["val_confidence"] >= MIN_CONFIDENCE) & (rules["val_lift"] >= MIN_LIFT)
rules["holds_conf_lift_only"] = (rules["val_confidence"] >= MIN_CONFIDENCE) & (rules["val_lift"] >= MIN_LIFT)

# Persistence baseline: candidate rules just BELOW the thresholds in the discovery year. If they 'hold' next year about as
# often, persistence says little; if far less often, passing the thresholds really selected stable patterns.
_, near = mine_rules(disc_baskets, min_conf=0.25, min_lift=1.5)
near = near[~((near["confidence"] >= MIN_CONFIDENCE) & (near["lift"] >= MIN_LIFT))]
near = add_validation(near)
near["holds_strict"] = (near["val_support"] >= MIN_SUPPORT) & (near["val_confidence"] >= MIN_CONFIDENCE) & (near["val_lift"] >= MIN_LIFT)
persist = pd.DataFrame({"rules": [len(rules), len(near)],
                        "meet all three thresholds next year %": [rules["holds_strict"].mean() * 100, near["holds_strict"].mean() * 100],
                        "meet confidence + lift only %": [rules["holds_conf_lift_only"].mean() * 100, np.nan]},
                       index=["rules that passed the thresholds", "baseline: near-miss rules (conf >= 0.25, lift >= 1.5)"]).round(1)
persist.to_csv(REP / "rule_persistence.csv"); display(persist)
lift_ratio = (rules["val_lift"] / rules["lift"]).describe(percentiles=[.1, .5, .9]).round(2)
print("Next-year lift / discovery lift:", lift_ratio[["10%", "50%", "90%"]].to_dict())

# Are the thresholds a sensible trade-off? Mine with other support / lift settings, validate each on the next year,
# and report how many rules survive and how much of the catalogue and of next year's baskets they cover.
val_l = val_lines.assign(item=val_lines["StockCode"].map(item_name))
val_items_by_inv = val_l.groupby("Invoice")["item"].agg(set)
grid_rows = []
for sup in [0.005, 0.01, 0.02]:
    items_s = disc_support[disc_support >= sup].index
    b_disc, b_val = basket_matrix(disc_lines, items_s), basket_matrix(val_lines, items_s)
    _, r_all = mine_rules(b_disc, min_support=sup, min_lift=2.0)
    for lift in [2.0, 3.0, 5.0]:
        r = r_all[r_all["lift"] >= lift]
        if r.empty: continue
        st = r.apply(lambda x: rule_stats(b_val, x["antecedents"], x["consequents"]), axis=1)
        hold = (st["val_support"] >= sup) & (st["val_confidence"] >= MIN_CONFIDENCE) & (st["val_lift"] >= lift)
        kept = r[hold.to_numpy()]
        ants = {a for t in kept["antecedents"] for a in t}
        fires = np.zeros(len(b_val), bool)
        for a, c in zip(kept["antecedents"], kept["consequents"]):
            fires |= b_val[list(a)].all(axis=1).to_numpy() & ~b_val[list(c)].all(axis=1).to_numpy()
        grid_rows.append({"min_support": sup, "min_lift": lift, "rules": len(r), "itemsets": r["itemset"].nunique(),
                          "hold_next_year_%": hold.mean() * 100, "products_with_a_validated_rule": len(ants),
                          "next_year_baskets_where_a_rule_fires_%": fires.mean() * 100})
threshold_grid = pd.DataFrame(grid_rows).round({"hold_next_year_%": 1, "next_year_baskets_where_a_rule_fires_%": 1})
threshold_grid.to_csv(REP / "rule_threshold_sensitivity.csv", index=False); display(threshold_grid)

# Sensitivity: anonymous invoices are much larger (2.4) - do they drive the rules? Re-mine on invoices WITH a Customer ID only.

id_support = item_support(id_lines)

main_pairs, id_pairs = set(zip(rules["antecedents"], rules["consequents"])), set(zip(id_rules["antecedents"], id_rules["consequents"]))

Do the rules hold next year? A rule holds only if it meets all three discovery thresholds again: support ≥ 1 %, confidence ≥ 0.4 and lift ≥ 3. The earlier versions checked only confidence and lift, which gave 86 %.

  • 59 % of the 598 rules hold. 85 % meet confidence and lift alone; most of the rest fall just below 1 % support in the second year.
  • Baseline: of 516 near-miss rules (confidence ≥ 0.25, lift ≥ 1.5, but below the thresholds in the discovery year), only 12 % reach the thresholds the next year. Passing the thresholds therefore really selects stable patterns. The pass mark (≥ 50 %, clearly above the baseline) is met. It was set after an earlier review had estimated about this rate, so it is a documented target rather than a blind one.
  • Strength holds too: next-year lift is typically 1.03 × the discovery lift (10th–90th percentile 0.82–1.34).

Threshold sensitivity (table above). This is sensitivity, not selection: the 1 % / 0.4 / 3 thresholds were fixed before mining, and the grid is scored on the validation year, so choosing from it would reuse that year. Confidence (0.4) and the 3-item limit were not varied.

  • Lift barely matters, because at 40 % confidence low-support items already have high lift. Support is the real trade-off.
  • At 0.5 % there are 4,465 rules, only 47 % hold, 301 products get a validated rule, and a validated rule fires in 72 % of next-year baskets (all of its "if" products present, its "then" product absent).
  • At 1 % (used) 59 % hold, 109 products are covered, and a rule fires in 59 % of baskets.
  • At 2 % only 62 rules and 24 products remain (31 % of baskets).

Anonymous baskets: re-mining on invoices with a Customer ID only gives 429 rules, and 90 % of them are in the main set. The large anonymous invoices add rules (35 % of the main rules need them to reach 1 % support) but do not create different ones.

5.4 Are the rules novel? Obvious variants vs cross-category associations¶

In [19]:
# Novelty: a rule is an obvious VARIANT if its products are the same product type that differ only in colour, design
# or size (e.g. JUMBO BAG OWLS vs JUMBO STORAGE BAG SUKI); otherwise it links different product types (CROSS-PRODUCT).
STYLE = r"\b(RED|PINK|BLUE|GREEN|WHITE|BLACK|IVORY|CREAM|PURPLE|YELLOW|ORANGE|SILVER|GOLD|PASTEL|ASSORTED|ROSES|POLKADOT|RETROSPOT|SPOTTY|SPOT|STRIPES?|FLORAL|SMALL|LARGE|JUMBO|MINI|SET|OF|AND|THE|WITH|DESIGN|\d+)\b"
# product-type nouns: two products that share one of these are the same kind of thing in a different design
TYPES = {"BAG", "CASE", "PLATE", "CUP", "BOWL", "NAPKIN", "MUG", "HEART", "LIGHT", "HOLDER", "BOX", "TIN", "CANDLE", "BOTTLE",
         "CLOCK", "SIGN", "FRAME", "CARD", "WRAP", "PEG", "DECORATION", "BUNTING", "TAPE", "PURSE", "UMBRELLA", "APRON", "CUSHION",
         "DOORMAT", "JAR", "TEACUP", "TRAY", "STICKER", "NOTEBOOK", "PENCIL", "CHALK", "LANTERN", "WREATH", "PARASOL", "DOORSTOP",
         "COASTER", "DRAWER", "KNOB", "BELL", "BUCKET", "BANNER", "GARLAND", "HANGER", "OVEN", "GLOVE", "TOWEL", "BASKET", "CRATE",
         "MAGNET", "PLAYHOUSE", "BALLOON", "STAND", "WALLET", "STRAW", "SPOON", "CUTLERY", "JIGSAW", "TISSUE", "TUMBLER", "VASE"}
words = lambda name: re.findall(r"[A-Z]{2,}", re.sub(STYLE, " ", str(name).upper()))
types_of = lambda name: {w[:-1] if w.endswith("S") and w[:-1] in TYPES else w for w in words(name)} & TYPES
def same_product(a, b):
    if types_of(a) & types_of(b):
        return True
    wa, wb = words(a), words(b)
    if len(wa) >= 2 and len(wb) >= 2 and (wa[:2] == wb[:2] or wa[-2:] == wb[-2:]):
        return True
    sa, sb = set(wa), set(wb)
    return len(sa & sb) / max(len(sa | sb), 1) >= 0.5

from itertools import combinations
classify = lambda a, c: ("variant (same product, other design)" if all(same_product(x, y) for x, y in combinations(a + c, 2))
                         else "cross-product")
rules["rule_type"] = [classify(a, c) for a, c in zip(rules["antecedents"], rules["consequents"])]
display(rules.groupby("rule_type").agg(rules=("lift", "size"), itemsets=("itemset", "nunique"), median_lift=("lift", "median"),
                                       holds_strict_pct=("holds_strict", lambda s: round(s.mean() * 100, 1))))
show = ["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift", "val_confidence", "val_lift"]
print("Strongest cross-product rules that met all three thresholds again in the following year (one direction per pair):")
cross = rules[(rules["rule_type"] == "cross-product") & rules["holds_strict"]].sort_values("confidence", ascending=False).drop_duplicates("itemset")
display(cross[show].head(12).round(3))
rules.to_csv(REP / "association_rules_evaluated.csv", index=False)

# Audit of the novelty classifier: a random sample of rules (one direction per itemset, up to 20 per type), labelled by hand.
# Hand rule: "variant" = the products are the same kind of item in another colour/design/size (a jumbo bag and a jumbo
# shopper are both large bags); "cross-product" = at least two different kinds of item (napkins and plates).
audit = pd.concat([g.sample(min(20, len(g)), random_state=RANDOM_STATE) for _, g in rules.drop_duplicates("itemset").groupby("rule_type")])
audit = audit.assign(rule=audit["antecedents"].apply(" + ".join) + "  ->  " + audit["consequents"].apply(" + ".join))
HAND_LABELS = ["variant", "cross-product", "cross-product", "cross-product", "cross-product", "cross-product", "variant", "cross-product", "variant", "cross-product", "variant", "cross-product", "variant", "cross-product", "cross-product", "variant", "cross-product", "cross-product", "cross-product", "cross-product", "variant", "variant", "cross-product", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant", "variant"]   # in the order of the sample below
audit["hand_label"] = HAND_LABELS
audit["classifier"] = audit["rule_type"].str.split(" ").str[0]
accuracy = (audit["classifier"] == audit["hand_label"]).groupby(audit["classifier"]).mean().rename("share_correct")
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 110); display(audit[["rule", "classifier", "hand_label"]]); pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 60)
def proportion_confint(k, n, z=1.96):   # Wilson score interval
    p = k / n; c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / (1 + z * z / n); h = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    return c - h, c + h
acc_tab = pd.DataFrame({"correct": (audit["classifier"] == audit["hand_label"]).groupby(audit["classifier"]).sum(),
                        "sampled": audit.groupby("classifier").size()})
acc_tab["share_correct"] = acc_tab["correct"] / acc_tab["sampled"]
acc_tab[["ci_95_low", "ci_95_high"]] = [proportion_confint(c, n) for c, n in zip(acc_tab["correct"], acc_tab["sampled"])]
display(acc_tab.round(2))
n_types = rules.drop_duplicates("itemset")["rule_type"].str.split(" ").str[0].value_counts()
est_cross = n_types["cross-product"] * accuracy["cross-product"] + n_types["variant"] * (1 - accuracy["variant"])
print(f"Estimated genuinely cross-product itemsets: about {est_cross:.0f} of {n_types.sum()} (classifier says {n_types['cross-product']}; "
      f"correct calls plus variants it misfiled). The hand labels are the author's own, so treat this as indicative.")
held = rules.drop_duplicates("itemset").groupby("rule_type")["holds_strict"].mean()
print("Share of itemsets whose rule holds next year, by type:", held.round(3).to_dict())
audit[["rule", "classifier", "hand_label"]].to_csv(REP / "novelty_audit.csv", index=False)

Evaluation against the Stage 0 criteria¶

Criterion Evidence Verdict
Valid Segments: next-year activity 96 % / 74 % / 65 % / 40 % in the predicted order; out-of-bag bootstrap ARI 0.92. But a plain RFM score ranks next-year activity better (AUC 0.765 vs 0.739, gap CI +0.018 to +0.034). Rules: 59 % meet all three thresholds again next year, against 12 % of near-miss rules; median lift changes by only +3 %. ✅ rules · ⚠️ segments: valid as descriptions, beaten as predictors
Novel 263 of the 325 itemsets are classified as variants (same product, other colour/design): expected, but useful for "complete the set" prompts. A hand audit of 40 sampled itemsets, labelled by the author (so indicative only), shows the classifier is right for 95 % of variants (CI 76–99 %) and 70 % of cross-product calls (CI 48–85 %). Counting cross-product itemsets misfiled as variants too, about 57 of the 325 are genuine cross-sells. These are customers buying matching-design sets across product types: red spotty napkins + cups → plates, Regency teacup and saucer → the matching cake stand, painted metal pears → bird ornament. But only 27 % of cross-product itemsets hold next year (variants: 62 %), so as a class the cross-sells are much less stable than the variants. Only the strongest ones (top of the table above) are reliable. Much of this follows the retailer's own collections, so it is better called a confirmation with numbers than a surprise. ⚠️ partly: novel patterns exist but are mostly unstable
Potentially useful Each segment has an action. S2 customers went on to spend £1.37 M the next year: the revenue a re-engagement campaign aims to keep, not money already lost. 352 validated rules (34 cross-product) cover 109 products, and a validated rule fires in 59 % of next-year baskets. That is only 109 of 4,047 products, which bounds the recommender's reach. ✅ with limited coverage
Understandable Segments described in plain words with member shares; rules shown as product names with confidence and lift. ✅

Iterations made (KDD loops back):

  • Round 1: the first evaluation used median-split labels (mislabelling S3 as "frequent"), lenient validity thresholds (99 % "held") and a word-matching novelty test that called key-fob variants cross-category.
  • Round 2: an independent review found that cleaning leaked across the split, return_rate double-counted, the "full thresholds" test skipped support (86 % → 59 %), the segments had no baseline, and the deployed app mislabelled its segments.
  • Round 3: the two Excel sheets overlapped (22,523 lines loaded twice), and the coverage figure counted rules that did not fully fire.

All were corrected, and Stage 5 now reports one criterion as not met and one as only partly met. See critiques/round_1.md – round_3.md.

🔍 Critic review — Interpretation and evaluation¶

Each stage was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on the Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process as defined by Fayyad, Piatetsky-Shapiro and Smyth, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on KDD and data mining. Review the Interpretation and evaluation stage of my retail KDD project below. Check it against everything this KDD stage requires. Focus especially on: whether the patterns were genuinely tested on data not used to find them, whether novelty and usefulness are argued rather than asserted, and whether loops back to earlier stages were considered. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Median-split labels mislabel S3; validity thresholds halved (too lenient); novelty test calls key-fob variants cross-category. Tertile labels + 'new' flag; strict validity test (86 % hold); product-type novelty test; app uses only strictly validated rules.
2 "86 % hold the full thresholds" skipped support (really 59 %); no segment baseline; novelty classifier unaudited. Strict three-threshold test + near-miss baseline (12 %); RFM baselines (clusters lose: 0.739 vs 0.765); hand audit.
3 Cross-product rules hold only ~27–34 % of the time; audit without CIs; coverage counted rules that did not fire. Claims rewritten (novel but mostly unstable); Wilson CIs, ≈ 57 genuine cross-sells; coverage = rules that fire (59 %).

Step 9 — Acting on the discovered knowledge¶

Fayyad step 9: use the knowledge directly, incorporate it into another system, or document and report it.

  • Segments: the app ships the validated discovery-year segmenter (the same model, the same 12-month window). It scores every customer on their most recent 12 months, so what was tested in 5.2 is what staff see.
  • Rules: re-mined on both years for current products. Each is flagged if the same rule was validated, and the app shows only validated rules by default.
  • Label check: the cell below re-profiles the deployed segments with the discovery cut-offs, to confirm each still matches its name.

import joblib
# Deploy the VALIDATED segmentation: the discovery-year model (12-month RFM window) scores every customer on the most
# recent 12 months. Same window length, same model, same names - so what was validated in 5.2 is what staff see.
snapshot = df["InvoiceDate"].max().normalize() + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
window_start = snapshot - pd.Timedelta(days=365)
recent = df[df["InvoiceDate"] >= window_start]
final_customers = customer_features(recent, returns[returns["InvoiceDate"] >= window_start], snapshot)
final_customers["cluster"] = segmenter.predict(final_customers[SEGMENT_FEATURES])
final_customers["segment"] = final_customers["cluster"].map(SEGMENT_OF)
final_customers["rfm_score_pct"] = ((final_customers["recency_days"].rank(ascending=False, pct=True) + final_customers["frequency"].rank(pct=True)
                                    + final_customers["monetary"].rank(pct=True)) / 3 * 100).round(0)

# Label check: do the deployed segments still look like their names? Profiles use the SAME tertile cut-offs as discovery.
final_prof = profile_segments(final_customers).rename(index=SEGMENT_OF).sort_index()
label_words = lambda s: [w for w in s.split() if not w.endswith("%") and w != "·"]
check = pd.DataFrame({"discovery_profile": prof["profile"], "deployed_profile": final_prof["profile"],
                      "discovery_customers": prof["customers"], "deployed_customers": final_prof["customers"],
                      "deployed_median_recency": final_prof["recency_days"], "deployed_median_tenure": final_prof["tenure_days"]})
check["labels_agree"] = [label_words(a)[:3] == label_words(b)[:3] for a, b in zip(check["discovery_profile"], check["deployed_profile"])]
check.to_csv(REP / "deployed_segment_label_check.csv"); display(check)
print("All deployed segments match their names." if check["labels_agree"].all() else "WARNING: a deployed segment no longer matches its name - revisit SEGMENT_ACTIONS")

# Rules for the app: re-mined on both years (more data, current products) and flagged if the same rule was validated.
full_lines = df[df["period"] != "after"]
full_support = item_support(full_lines)
_, final_rules = mine_rules(basket_matrix(full_lines, full_support[full_support >= MIN_SUPPORT].index))
validated = set(zip(rules.loc[rules["holds_strict"], "antecedents"], rules.loc[rules["holds_strict"], "consequents"]))
final_rules["validated_next_year"] = [(a, c) in validated for a, c in zip(final_rules["antecedents"], final_rules["consequents"])]
final_rules["rule_type"] = [classify(a, c) for a, c in zip(final_rules["antecedents"], final_rules["consequents"])]
out_rules = final_rules.assign(antecedent=final_rules["antecedents"].apply(" + ".join), consequent=final_rules["consequents"].apply(" + ".join))[
    ["antecedent", "consequent", "support", "confidence", "lift", "validated_next_year", "rule_type"]].sort_values("confidence", ascending=False).round(4)
out_rules.to_csv(APP / "rules.csv", index=False)
final_customers.reset_index().to_csv(APP / "customer_segments.csv", index=False)
joblib.dump(segmenter, APP / "segmenter.joblib")
meta = {"created": datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"), "k": K, "segment_features": SEGMENT_FEATURES,
        "snapshot": str(snapshot.date()), "window": f"{window_start.date()} .. {(snapshot - pd.Timedelta(days=1)).date()} (12 months)",
        "segments": SEGMENT_ACTIONS, "cluster_to_segment": {str(k): v for k, v in SEGMENT_OF.items()},
        "profiles": final_prof.drop(columns="revenue").reset_index(names="segment").to_dict(orient="records"),
        "versions": {"python": platform.python_version(), "numpy": np.__version__, "pandas": pd.__version__, "scikit-learn": sklearn.__version__}}
(APP / "metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps(meta, indent=2, default=str), encoding="utf-8")
print(f"{len(final_customers):,} customers active in the last 12 months segmented | {len(out_rules):,} rules "

APP_CODE = r"""
import json
from pathlib import Path
import joblib
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
st.set_page_config(page_title="Retail insights", page_icon="🛍️")

@st.cache_resource
def load():
    meta = json.loads((HERE / "metadata.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    rules = pd.read_csv(HERE / "rules.csv")
    rules["ante_set"] = rules["antecedent"].str.split(" + ", regex=False).apply(frozenset)
    rules["cons_set"] = rules["consequent"].str.split(" + ", regex=False).apply(frozenset)
    customers = pd.read_csv(HERE / "customer_segments.csv", dtype={"Customer ID": str})
    return meta, rules, customers, joblib.load(HERE / "segmenter.joblib")

meta, rules, customers, segmenter = load()
st.title("🛍️ Customer segments & product recommendations")
st.caption(f"Online Retail II · {len(customers):,} customers active in {meta['window']} · {len(rules):,} association rules")
seg_info = meta["segments"]

recs, lookup, new_cust, overview = st.tabs(["Product recommendations", "Customer lookup", "Segment a customer", "Segments overview"])
with recs:
    only_valid = st.checkbox("Only rules that met support, confidence and lift again in the following year", value=True)
    hide_variants = st.checkbox("Hide colour/design variants of the same product (show cross-sell only)", value=False)
    pool = rules[rules["validated_next_year"]] if only_valid else rules
    if hide_variants:
        pool = pool[pool["rule_type"] == "cross-product"]
    products = sorted({p for s in pool["ante_set"] for p in s})
    basket = set(st.multiselect("Products in the customer's basket", products, default=products[:1]))
    hits = pool[pool["ante_set"].apply(lambda a: a <= basket) & pool["cons_set"].apply(lambda c: not (c & basket))]
    if not basket:
        st.info("Pick one or more products.")
    elif hits.empty:
        st.info("No association for this basket - every rule needs ALL of its 'if' products in the basket.")
    else:
        st.dataframe(hits[["antecedent", "consequent", "confidence", "lift", "rule_type"]].head(15), hide_index=True)
        top = hits.iloc[0]
        st.success(f"Suggest **{top['consequent']}**: bought in {top['confidence']:.0%} of baskets containing "
                   f"{top['antecedent']} ({top['lift']:.1f}x more often than average).")
with lookup:
    cid = st.text_input("Customer ID", value=customers["Customer ID"].iloc[0])
    row = customers[customers["Customer ID"] == cid.strip()]
    if row.empty:
        st.warning("Customer not found (only customers who ordered in the last 12 months are segmented).")
    else:
        r = row.iloc[0]; s = seg_info[r["segment"]]
        st.subheader(s["name"]); st.write(f"**Recommended action:** {s['action']}")
        c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
        c1.metric("Days since last order", int(r["recency_days"])); c2.metric("Orders (12 months)", int(r["frequency"])); c3.metric("Spend, 12 months (GBP)", f"{r['monetary']:,.0f}")
        st.write(f"**RFM score:** better than {int(r['rfm_score_pct'])} % of customers. Use it to rank customers *within* a segment "
                 "(it predicts next-year activity slightly better than the segment alone).")
with new_cust:
    st.write("Enter the customer's activity over the **last 12 months** (the window the segments were built and validated on).")
    c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
    rec = c1.number_input("Days since last order", 0, 365, 30)
    freq = c2.number_input("Orders in the last 12 months", 1, 500, 3)
    mon = c3.number_input("Spend in the last 12 months (GBP)", 1.0, 1e6, 500.0)
    cluster = int(segmenter.predict(pd.DataFrame([{"recency_days": rec, "frequency": freq, "monetary": mon}]))[0])
    seg = meta["cluster_to_segment"][str(cluster)]
    st.subheader(seg_info[seg]["name"]); st.write(f"**Recommended action:** {seg_info[seg]['action']}")
with overview:
    st.write(f"Segment profiles for customers active in {meta['window']} (medians; labels use the discovery-year tertiles).")
    st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame(meta["profiles"]), hide_index=True)
    pick = st.selectbox("Export a segment's customer list (ranked by RFM score)", sorted(seg_info))
    lst = customers[customers["segment"] == pick].sort_values("rfm_score_pct", ascending=False)
    st.download_button(f"Download {pick} ({len(lst):,} customers)", lst.to_csv(index=False), f"segment_{pick}.csv")
"""
(APP / "app.py").write_text(APP_CODE.strip() + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
v = meta["versions"]
(APP / "requirements.txt").write_text(f"streamlit>=1.40\nscikit-learn=={v['scikit-learn']}\nnumpy=={v['numpy']}\npandas=={v['pandas']}\njoblib\n")
compile(APP_CODE, "app.py", "exec")
print("App files:", sorted((p.name, f"{p.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB") for p in APP.iterdir()))
print(f"When deploying, choose Python {v['python'][:4]} so the pinned versions install and the segmenter loads.")

When deploying, choose Python 3.13 so the pinned versions install and the segmenter loads.

Deploy (free): put artifacts/app/ in your GitHub repo → share.streamlit.io → Create app → kdd/artifacts/app/app.py; pick the Python version printed above. To change segment names or actions, edit SEGMENT_ACTIONS and re-run.

What the app does:

  • Recommendations. Staff enter the whole basket, and a rule fires only when all of its "if" products are in it, so the confidence shown applies to that basket. A checkbox hides colour/design variants to show cross-sells only.
  • Customer lookup. Shows the customer's segment and action plus an RFM score (percentile), the better tool for ranking customers within a segment (5.2).
  • Segment a customer. The inputs are explicitly last-12-month figures, the window the model was built and validated on.
  • Segments overview. Shows the deployed segments' own profiles, and exports each segment's customer list ranked by RFM score for a campaign.
  • Label check (above). All four deployed segments still match their names, with the same majority labels and the same order: S1 682, S2 1,176, S3 784 and S4 1,608 customers active in the last 12 months.

Consolidating the knowledge¶

  • Agreement with prior knowledge: the segments match classic RFM intuition — a small group of recent, frequent buyers carries most revenue (17 % of customers → 64 % of revenue) — and an RFM score does better at prediction. This builds trust in the result and limits its novelty.
  • What is new: some design collections are bought together across product types, strongly and stably (red spotty napkins + cups → plates: confidence 84 %, still 90 % the next year). For a giftware merchandiser this suggests organising the web shop by collection (all "red retrospot" items together) as well as by product type, and bundling matching items. Most cross-product associations, however, do not repeat the next year, so only the validated ones should be promoted.
  • Conflicts to watch: most rules are colour/design variants; promoting them only helps if the product page doesn't already show all colours.
  • Measuring the effect: run each segment action and the recommendation tab as an A/B test with a random 20 % hold-out per segment. Compare next-quarter purchase rate and basket size; this ties the result back to the Stage 0 goals.
  • Maintenance (owner: the marketing analyst):
    • every quarter, re-mine on a rolling 12-month window;
    • validate each mined set on the following 12 months once they are available, the same design as this notebook, so validation lags the mining by a year;
    • in between, track monthly how often the published rules still meet their thresholds on the latest 12 months, and alert if that falls below 50 % or a segment's size moves by more than 25 %;
    • re-run the label check before publishing.
  • Data governance: the app holds customer IDs with their spend. That is acceptable for this public research dataset, but a real deployment needs access control and a retention rule.
